L’effet de la pandémie se fait grandemen: The pandemic's effect on students is being felt deeply: dropping out, poor grades and more.

The pandemic's effect on students is being felt deeply: dropping out, poor grades and more. Many are abandoning their postsecondary studies because they are discouraged by online learning. Starting tomorrow, universities and CEGEPs will partially reopen. But while we wait for a full reopening, is it time to rethink how we teach at CEGEP and university?
« Si tu n’es pas bien préparé en ligne,: “If you’re not well prepared online, it doesn’t work, whereas in class it’s easier to improvise and adapt. Being online taught me to stop cutting corners,” says professor Karoline Truchon. She has taught communication in social sciences at the Université du Québec en Outaouais for two years, which means she will have spent most of her career as a professor online. “For me, online is another form of presence,” she explains. What she rejects is the traditional lecture accompanied by a PowerPoint presentation.
« Il s’agit d’enseigner, pas de donner u: “It’s about teaching, not giving a lecture,” says the professor. “It already doesn’t work in a classroom, and it works even less online,” Ms. Truchon laments, pointing out that without interaction, students tune out, don’t feel motivated and don’t feel like they belong to a group. “It’s hard for students, but professors bear some of the responsibility,” she concludes. Truchon, who holds a doctorate in anthropology, applies this transparency across the board with her class. “In everyday life, we can hide plenty of things, but on screen, you can’t lie,” she believes. Before every class, she therefore starts a routine that helps her be fully present and available for her students: taking several deep breaths, positioning her screen a certain way, drinking a tea, and so on.
Si elle se sent mal, elle n’hésite pas à: If she isn’t feeling well, she doesn’t hesitate to cancel her class and tell her students. They seem to appreciate this honesty enormously, and it leads them to share their own feelings with their teacher. In class, everything runs through technology, with dynamic lessons in which every last detail is planned in advance. The virtual class is entirely scripted, every lesson and every activity, which allows her to handle the unexpected. To achieve this, Ms. Truchon uses a range of tools to fuel reflection and discussion: custom microsites, an interactive whiteboard, highlighted readings, audio comments, analysis grids and visual diagrams, webinars, virtual guests and pre-recorded videos, and more. The professor also applies the principles of participatory design and doesn’t hesitate to break the rhythm to keep students alert and interested.
« Chaque semaine, je me réinvente pour v: “Every week, I reinvent myself to figure out how I’m going to deliver the content, but in a way that will connect them through this screen.” For the professor, the effort is worth it, and it is part of a teacher’s workload, particularly in preparing a course. “It’s true that I put a lot of time into it, and I love it. I see the effect in the class, it feeds me and I love seeing them get into it. And I can see that they’re learning.” While her virtual approach yields excellent results, Ms. Truchon believes every professor has to find their own way to hook students. “I have a colleague who talks for several hours, and it goes very well. His tool is speech; that requires a different kind of preparation. The students like us both because we give it our all,” she explains.
Comme la plupart des professeurs, Karine: Like most professors, Karine Deshayes, a senior lecturer in intercultural management at HEC Montréal, has been teaching virtually for almost a year. The professor, who teaches interpersonal skills, feared she wouldn’t be able to adequately recreate the classroom experience online. She says she is happy to see that very few students have dropped out of the program.
Ses étudiants ont en moyenne 18 ans. « L: Her students are 18 on average. “The pandemic has shown us that the approach of kindness and support within the program has been quite beneficial,” she observes. While motivation is often thought to be mostly the student’s responsibility, Ms. Deshayes believes that professors play a major role in keeping students when classes are held online. “For years, we weren’t used to doing care, to taking the time to connect with students,” she says. “And we’re discovering it. It takes coaches, more than traditional teachers.”
Empathie, flexibilité, soutien – cette f: Empathy, flexibility, support: this way of teaching requires effort and willingness on the part of professors. “We have to move away from the traditional way of teaching, innovating on our traditional methods, to go and meet students where they are,” she believes. To get her students to participate, she asks them a lot of questions. “I start every class by asking them how they’re doing. It’s not just for show,” says the professor, who believes it is essential to build a relationship of trust.
Elle demande également aux étudiants de: She also asks students to send her an introductory video. “It let me see everyone’s personality, take notes, take the pulse of my class.” In class, hands-on experience is also important, with role plays and scenarios that sharpen students’ creativity. Ms. Deshayes also favours the flipped classroom, a teaching approach in which students prepare their lessons at home through readings and research, before the material is covered in class through activities that allow them to review and explore the topics in greater depth.
Les évaluations ont aussi été revues, le: Evaluations have also been revisited, with the traditional model of a midterm and a final exam set aside. Like professor Karoline Truchon, Karine Deshayes works with other experts who are invited into her class. “I go find people who are more specialized than I am in certain areas so I can offer the best,” she says. Virtual teaching requires no travel for guests, which, according to the professors, makes things easier.

Les méthodes d’enseignement de Karoline: The teaching methods of Karoline Truchon and Karine Deshayes shake up traditional university teaching. Is it therefore time to rethink who teaches at university, and how? “I don’t know whether my colleagues see their job the same way I do,” says Ms. Deshayes. For her part, Ms. Truchon believes that, above all, you have to “love teaching and love the subject you teach and, above all, want to teach.”
Pour l’anthropologue, un bon professeur: For the anthropologist, a good university professor must above all be a good educator. The problem is that many university professors put academic research ahead of teaching. “You have to carry teaching the way you carry your research,” she says. At CEGEP, the educational setting seems better suited to students’ needs, with smaller classes and professors more devoted to teaching and to students’ success. Gisela Frias, who teaches geography at Dawson College, is also the coordinator of North South Studies, an applied social sciences program that departs from the traditional pre-university program and is instead built on care.
La professeure soulève une question plus: The professor raises a broader question: that of entirely rethinking teaching by adapting programs and pedagogy to the circumstances. “I think it’s not enough for teachers to adapt their courses. We haven’t changed pedagogy as a whole, knowing that education is now delivered online,” she says.
Johanna Okker, professeure de sciences h: Johanna Okker, a humanities professor at John Abbott College, draws on decolonial practices to improve students’ experience. “I recognize that the things I do to take care of my students are practices that have existed in Indigenous communities for centuries.
C’est une partie essentielle du réseau d: It’s an essential part of the community’s network of support and learning,” she explains. Ms. Okker adds that checking in with students by forming a circle at the start of the session, where everyone can speak in turn, is a fundamental value of Indigenous teaching. “Because of time constraints, that’s not necessarily possible with 40 students, but I adapt the approach,” says the professor. By listening to her students, Ms. Okker was able to revise her course plan and adapt it accordingly.
« Ce n’était pourtant pas grand-chose. I: “It wasn’t much, though. It was a topic, changing a due date,” she says. “One student told me that if more professors did this kind of thing, student burnout rates would drop considerably. These small interventions we make as teachers can have a big impact,” she says.
Au First Nations Regional Adult Educatio: At the First Nations Regional Adult Education Center in Kahnawake, Fran Beauvais works as an academic advisor. Here, teaching is almost tailor-made, with staff particularly attuned to students and their needs. “Students arrive with a goal, and part of their success is based on the support we give them. The responsibility doesn’t fall on them alone,” she explains.
« Je pense que nous devons vraiment comp: “I think we really have to understand how we can help them so that they can succeed,” says Ms. Beauvais of the difficulties caused by the pandemic.
Pour les étudiants, la meilleure façon d: For students, the best way to avoid dropping out is the support of a community. Gabrielle Allard is grateful for her friendship with Elisa-Maria Lutic, her mentor. The two students met through HEC’s mentorship program. This year, to meet relational needs, each student in the preparatory year, a one-year program for students who don’t have a college diploma or who have an atypical background, is paired with a senior student. Gabrielle, who arrived in Quebec last July and is starting her first year of a bachelor’s degree, has a rather small social circle.
Sa relation avec Elisa-Maria, qui est fi: Her relationship with Elisa-Maria, who is a graduating student and knows student life very well, has helped her enormously to fit in. “I ask her all my questions, like how to register for a course,” says Gabrielle. Having been through it herself, Elisa-Maria also knows the workload, the courses and the projects, and can offer advice. “It’s useful, both academically and socially,” Gabrielle explains. “We talk, we ask each other how it’s going. It’s good to have someone to talk to, to have at least one friend.” Elisa-Maria says she benefits just as much from the relationship. “It’s truly a pleasure for us to share our experience,” she says. The 21-year-old loves meeting new people and getting involved in student life, something online education makes difficult. She misses the buzzing life of campus, and above all regrets not being able to attend the graduation ceremony with her classmates and her family, who live in France. “Sometimes it’s hard on morale,” she confides. She nonetheless remains optimistic in the midst of this unusual time. Despite the absence of student parties and events, there are still plenty of distractions.
« Oui, on procrastine quand même si on e: “Yes, you still procrastinate when you’re at home, and you go to bed late!” says Elisa-Maria, laughing. To stay motivated, she keeps up a pace and a routine that make her want to work. “Before, if I didn’t have class the next day, I wouldn’t get up early,” says the student, who has become an early riser to be more productive. She believes, however, that it’s important to go easy on yourself and not feel bad about not studying or spending time on your phone. “Don’t hesitate to do something else outside your classes. Clearing your head is important too,” says Elisa-Maria, who likes learning new choreographies on TikTok and cooking. Gabrielle, who never experienced university life as it existed before the pandemic, suggests reaching out to a few people and getting to know one or two other students in the same course or program.
« C’est parfois difficile de trouver l’i: “It’s sometimes hard to find information, or even just to know what’s going on. It’s not like you can run into someone in the hallway who could tell you,” she says. “I was very shy at first, and I didn’t want to write in the groups with 200 students, but through group projects, I had a few teammates I kept in touch with, and we built an online friendship.” This closeness with her classmates breaks the isolation, but also lets them help each other in class.
« Pour nous aider si on ne trouve pas le: “To help us out if we can’t find the link, for example,” she says, laughing. While the educators we spoke with have adapted to online teaching, all agree that students are eager to return to campus.
